t: “I’ve seen this before...”
q: When you encounter something that seems familiar, you’re likely to handle it in the way you handled it before. Easy peasy. Your previous experience becomes the scaffolding for the solution.

A sales manager sees declining numbers. He thinks back to a customer visit the week before, when one rep wasn’t particularly crisp on the close. He brings in training for a refresher on selling techniques.
The first plausible explanation of a problem gives us something to latch onto. If it’s X, I can do Y… and off you go, charting a path to the solution.
Anchoring. The first explanation becomes the reference point for the thinking that follows. Once you have that working theory, you start noticing the evidence that supports it.
Expertise. The IT guy will see a systems problem. The Six Sigma black belt will see a process problem. The expertise leads the witness - and becomes the lens through which people view the problem.

But acting on it means investing in it - with budget, people, time, or all three. And the more you invest in the diagnosis that drove the solution, the harder it becomes to undo if the diagnosis turns out to be wrong.
But where you do have the power to persuade, asking “What else could it be?” can save you from delivering a really elegant solution to a problem you don’t have.

t: You Can't Think Clearly in a Room Full of Noise
q: It took me a long time to realize the problem was never a lack of information. It was too much noise, and no quiet place to actually think inside of.
Thinking is not the same thing as consuming information. Thinking is what happens after you stop consuming, when you actually sit with what you’ve taken in and let it settle into something usable.
A mind that is constantly reacting to input has no room left to evaluate it. You cannot judge something clearly while you’re still being hit by it.
You’re not stupid. You’re just depleted, and depletion looks a lot like confusion from the inside.
Silence, on purpose, before you decide anything that matters. Not silence as an escape. Silence as a workspace.
The people who seem to make good decisions quickly aren’t smarter. They’ve just built the habit of thinking before they consume, instead of consuming until a decision falls out by accident.
Most of the time, you’ll find you haven’t really thought at all. You’ve just been absorbing.

t: Working With Parents Who Only Value Top Achievement For Their Child
q: I’ve seen students who have worked very hard, and who have achieved really good results, only to be met with a parent’s disappointment.

What parents often don’t realise is that this kind of pressure can create fear and perfectionism, and can lead to their child believing that nothing they do can ever enough. And that mindset often leads to worse performance on future tests.
When I come across this, I don’t try to win the argument. I’ve learned that pushing too hard only makes parents dig their heels in and stick to their position more.
I’ve found that if I’m specific about where I praise a student’s work, it usually feels more credible to parents who value measurable achievement.
Some parents believe that if their child struggles, something is wrong, so I point out that the topic being studied is often challenging for most students.

I help students to separate their identity from their grades by reminding them that they are not their score, and a grade only measures their performance on one day. It can never measure their intelligence or their worth, but sadly this is a message they rarely hear at home.

I’m aware of when the healthiest thing to do is to stop trying to convince the parent about why top grades don’t fully show the progress a student has made. I’ve learned to state my case once, clearly, and then let it rest.

q: A minute of rest isn’t wasted just because it looks empty. And a lot of minutes that look busy are wasted. What matters is what a minute is doing.

But the easiest win by a long way is just to leave out the things that can’t justify being let back in. And the clearest example I know is the exercise book.
In an hour’s lesson that’s an eighth to a fifth of the lesson, every lesson. At four lessons a week for a year it’s around twenty hours per class, which is about five weeks of maths.

t: What Does Her Future Hold?
q: I am thinking about what will live inside it by the time she is old enough to hold one. What is her world going to be? The phone can’t tell me. Nobody can.

Now the work can be done by something that is not the student, logged in as the student. The question was never really whether AI could do the work. It is whether we have built a school where the work is worth doing yourself.

t: The Manager Who Was Too Good at His Job
q: Umbrella managers shield a team from the endless stream of requests, distractions and shifting priorities coming from above, allowing them to focus more efficiently on the work. Funnel managers simply pass them on.

If you go on holiday or leave the company and your team collapses, you didn’t do your job.

t: The Manager Who Never Got the Manual
q: There is a job in almost every organisation that combines the highest direct influence on employee wellbeing, team productivity, and talent retention with some of the least investment in formal preparation.

t: The Internet Doesn't Know How to Be CEO
q: The Internet gave us a thousand contradictory answers. AI can now read all thousand, reconcile the contradictions, sand off the sharp edges, and hand us a polished synthesis. It is masterful at caveats.

t: If Marriages Are Lasting Longer, How Can We Make Them Last for Life?

q: Atomization is a term used by some to describe the process of decomposing materials into the smallest necessary units, and ensuring that each new atom is explicitly taught one at a time.

t: Why You Should Never Ask Students To Apologize
q: When you know the apology you’ve received was prompted by a person in authority, it means nothing. It’s proof, even, that the apology wasn’t real.
The indignity of having to listen to your tormentor’s forced apology is one reason why restorative justice practices not only don’t work, but often cause deep resentment.
If the apology doesn’t originate from within the misbehaving student, then it isn’t sincere. It’s a hoop to jump through to get the teacher off their back.
The wronged party knows this. It’s all a charade meant only to satisfy the teacher, who can then carry on self-satisfied and convinced they handled it well.
Accountability in the classroom can only come from a predetermined consequence. It’s the certainty of breaking a rule that harmed another that most effectively causes a contrite heart.

Understanding how their actions affect others often triggers a desire to make amends. Done right, and over time, accountability causes the kind of self-reflection and empathy that triggers an apology.
It’s prompted by a consistently followed classroom management plan.

t: When Math Stops Being the Measure of Intelligence
q: What we regard as intelligence is partly a function of scarcity. Mathematical ability has historically carried such prestige because it is difficult and relatively rare among humans.
Technology has done this before. Calculators reduced the value of doing long calculations by hand. Spreadsheets reduced the value of constructing financial models manually.

In other words, the CEO’s intelligence has always depended less on personally producing every answer than on knowing what to do with the answers other people produce. AI pushes more of us in that direction.

But none of those activities settles the question. Someone still has to decide which considerations matter most, reconcile conflicting information, understand the people involved, and act under uncertainty.

If analytical horsepower becomes abundant, the scarce forms of intelligence inside an organization may increasingly be the ability to frame the right problem, exercise judgment, connect ideas across domains, recognize good work, understand people, and turn knowledge into action.
The scarce capability will increasingly be not producing the technically correct answer, but applying judgment to it: What question should we be asking? Which answers matter?

t: Turning Direction into Delivered Work

t: The Top Idea in Your Mind
q: I think most people have one top idea in their mind at any given time.
Which means it's a disaster to let the wrong idea become the top one in your mind.
The problem is that once you start raising money, raising money becomes the top idea in your mind.
You can't directly control where your thoughts drift. If you're controlling them, they're not drifting. But you can control them indirectly, by controlling what situations you let yourself get into.
These too are engaging in the wrong way: they have the same velcro-like shape as genuinely interesting ideas, but without the substance.
Someone who does you an injury hurts you twice: first by the injury itself, and second by taking up your time afterward thinking about it.
But it's easy to figure this out: just take a shower. What topic do your thoughts keep returning to?

t: The Fastest Way to Lose Credibility With a New Leader
q: When a new leader arrives, most team members instinctively shift into impression-management mode. They highlight their significant accomplishments, position their skills, and look for opportunities to demonstrate their value.
Seasoned leaders have seen this before. They know that nearly everyone they meet in the first 100 days is auditioning. And because they know it, they discount it.
The team member who leads with their resume sparks skepticism, not confidence. The very behavior intended to build credibility erodes it.

The most credible thing a team member can do in the early days of a leadership transition is to identify what the organization really needs — even when that assessment is inconvenient for them personally.
They have put the organization before themselves. They have separated their recommendation from their fate. That is instantly and unmistakably credible.
Most people spend that window trying to look good. The ones who earn real trust spend it trying to be useful.

t: The Detention Paradox
q: The problem wasn’t that sanctions didn’t work but that they only appeared to work for some students.

But using the behaviour of this group to judge whether detention deters students in general is like evaluating the effectiveness of speed cameras by only interviewing drivers who’ve been caught speeding. The most persistent offenders are, by definition, unrepresentative.
Experimental research on ‘third-party punishment’ has found that when people see someone punished for violating a norm, it changes their beliefs about what others approve of.

Keizer and colleagues called this the ‘spreading of disorder’ — a phenomenon all too common in schools. Observing violations, particularly those that go unsanctioned, reduces the likelihood of rules being followed in general.

There’s little reason to think that making a detention two hours long rather than one will somehow transform behaviour. Excessive or arbitrary punishment undermines the legitimacy on which effective discipline depends.
A rule which is repeatedly broken without consequence stops functioning as a rule. Students quickly learn what will be tolerated and adjust the behaviour accordingly.

So, here’s my conclusion: detentions only work for those kids who go with the flow. It would be obviously wrong to punish children who always behave well and kids who, like my younger self, always seem to do the wrong thing are unlikely to be persuaded by consequences they routinely fail to see coming.

t: Pick Up the Shovel
q: There’s a difference between working hard and working diligently. Working hard is about effort. Working diligently is about effort applied consistently toward something that matters.

Diligence is the willingness to keep doing the right work, even when the payoff isn’t immediate, because the work you do today isn’t just producing today’s result; it’s also producing the person you become in the process.
Covey wasn’t teaching his son how to mow a lawn. He was teaching him how to take responsibility for a result.
But if we’re always telling our kids exactly what to do, when to do it and how to do it, we can accidentally teach them that responsibility means following instructions.
And it’s not enough that they see you leave for the office. Your kids need to see you doing things around the house.
The important part is to let them own the work. Don’t hover. Don’t take over.
Because the greatest gift we can give our kids isn’t a life without difficult work. It’s the confidence to believe they can do difficult things.

It takes systems, the careful application of systems, the review of systems, and the chucking out of systems that simply don’t work.
At the risk of sounding pithy, it means keeping the main thing - what’s happening in classrooms, in front of kids - the main thing.

t: On Being a Human
q: No human can be a means to an end. Every human must be the end for any other human.

You have taken an eternal thing, a human soul, and used that soul as a means to some selfish end. Achilles fractures the Greek army to get his prize back, and many die, including his friend Patroclus.
No man should treat women as “other,” because the totality of humanity is woman and man.

q: AI is both a huge opportunity for learning and a huge risk to learning at the same time. AI in schools is not one thing; it is a source of power to do many things—some great, some horrible.
But I did regularly see students open their search browser, ask a question, and copy the “AI Overview” summary without questioning it or—as far as I could tell—usually even reading it.

I have seen screenshots of computers in New York and L.A. (where most AI is banned in K–12 schools) that show the AI summary in Google Search still alive and active. The bans do not seem to have ruled out the biggest risk to learning I saw on the tour.

I saw targeted instructional tools use AI to give students massively more practice and feedback on their writing than the most industrious human teacher could deliver in a week. It didn’t eliminate the need for teachers to also read and provide feedback on student work, but it did give teachers a huge assist in a laborious instructional job.

It is hard to come to a consensus definition about what AI even is. Even if you could get large groups of people to agree on definitions, the technology is changing so rapidly that they’d need near-constant revision.
